title: SQL and NoSQL
summary: Relational databases and the main kinds of NoSQL store, what each is good at, and how to choose between them.

blocks.p: Almost every system needs a database, and there are many kinds. Relational databases have been the default for decades. NoSQL stores promise easier scaling or a better fit for some shapes of data.
The choice shapes everything after it: how you model data, which queries are cheap, and how you scale. Choosing well starts with how your data will be read.

A relational database stores data in tables of rows and columns, with a fixed schema. Related data lives in separate tables and is linked by keys. A query in SQL can **join** tables, filter, sort and group, all in the database. The model comes from [Edgar Codd's 1970 paper](https://doi.org/10.1145/362384.362685).
Relational databases also offer **transactions**: a group of changes that happens completely or not at all. The transactions lesson covers this.
NoSQL is a loose name for databases that are not relational. The main kinds:

list: **Key-value.** Get and put a value by its key, and little else. Very fast, very simple.
**Document.** Each record is a document, such as JSON, that can hold nested data. Data that is read together is stored together.
**Wide-column.** Rows grouped by a partition key and sorted within it, spread over many machines. Built for very large write volumes.
**Graph.** Nodes and the relationships between them, for queries that follow many links.

blocks.p: An order page needs the order, its line items and each item's product. Here are three ways to read it. The first is a common mistake: one query for the order, then a query per item from the app. The second joins the tables in one query. The third stores the whole order as one document.

blocks.caption: Reading one order with three items, with a 1 ms round trip to the database. Count the round trips in each version.

blocks.p: The document is fastest for this page because it was designed for this page. Ask a different question, such as total sales per product, and the relational version groups compact rows from an indexed line-items table, while the document store must scan or unwind whole orders.

blocks.p: Start with a relational database unless you have a reason not to. It answers questions you didn't plan for. Move a specific workload to a NoSQL store when you know its access pattern and need that store's scale or speed.

list: **The lines have blurred.** PostgreSQL stores and indexes JSON documents in its [jsonb type](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/datatype-json.html). Several document stores now support multi-document transactions.

**DynamoDB starts from access patterns.** Amazon's [NoSQL design guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/bp-general-nosql-design.html) says to list your application's access patterns before designing the table, the reverse of relational design.
**MongoDB favours embedding.** Its [data modeling guide](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/data-modeling/) recommends storing data that is accessed together in the same document.
**Watch for query-per-item loops.** The first version in the figure is common in code that uses an ORM. Check how many queries a page sends, not only how long each takes.
Relational databases store tables with a fixed schema and answer any query with joins.
NoSQL stores trade query flexibility for a data model that fits known access patterns.
Document stores keep data that is read together in one place.
Default to relational, and choose NoSQL for a known access pattern that needs it.
